summary: Hiroshi Araki is a scholar in Japanology and Buddhist studies who completed undergraduate and graduate studies, including a PhD (2013), at Kyoto University. He taught at Osaka University and served as Professor at the International Research Center for Japanese Studies (2010–2025).
Hiroshi Deguchi studied at the University of Tokyo from circa 1948 to 1953 and held a post at Hokkaido University from circa 1965 to 1988.
Hiroshi Kanaseki worked in history and archaeology after studying at Kyoto University from circa 1949 to 1953. He held a post at Tenri University from circa 1967 to 1998.

Hiroshi Kanno, a scholar of Buddhist studies and Sinology, studied at the University of Tokyo. He served as Director at Soka University (1997) and at the International Research Institute for Advanced Buddhology (circa 2002–2009).

Hiroshi Kuroda is an Indology and philosophy scholar who completed doctoral coursework at Kyoto University (circa 1974–1976). He served as an assistant professor at Osaka Gakuin Junior College (circa 1983–1990) and Osaka Gakuin University (circa 1983–1993).

Hiroshi Marui is an Indology and philosophy scholar who studied at the University of Tokyo, Savitribai Phule Pune University, and under Albrecht Wezler. He served as assistant professor at the University of Tokyo (1992, 1995, 1999–2018).
Hiroshi Maruyama is a scholar in Indology and other fields who was attested in 1987 as a professor at Osaka University and head of the Ayurveda Research Society.
Hiroshi Nemoto is a scholar in Tibetology, Buddhist studies, and Indology. He earned his MA at Hiroshima University, where he is attested as a professor from 2015 to 2016.
Hiroshi Yamashita specializes in Indology and religious studies. He studied at the University of Madras and was an associate professor at Tohoku University (attested 1996–1999).
Hirotomo Teranishi succeeded Hiroshi Kanno in 2009 and served as director at Soka University (attested 2010–2011).
Hiroyuki Kato was a scholar of philosophy and other fields who held posts at Bansho Shirabesho (circa 1860–1862), the Kaisei School (circa 1869–1877), and the University of Tokyo (circa 1877–1893).
Hisanosuke Izui was a linguist who studied at Kyoto University and held a post at Kyoto Sangyo University from circa 1968 to 1983.

Hisao Inagaki was a Buddhist studies scholar who studied at Ryukoku, Kobe, and London universities. He taught Japanese Buddhism at SOAS (1969–1981) and served as Professor at Ryukoku University (1981–1998).

Hisao Kanaseki, a Buddhist studies scholar, studied at Doshisha University. He was a professor at Kobe University (circa 1965–1973), professor emeritus at Tokyo Metropolitan University (circa 1973–1982), and professor at Komazawa University (circa 1982–1989).

Hisao Takahashi, an Indology and Buddhist studies scholar, studied at Taisho University under Ryukai Mano. Taisho University posts include assistant (attested 1977–1982), lecturer (attested 1995), and professor (attested 2004–2010).

Hisashi Matsumura is a scholar in Buddhist studies and Indology who held posts at the Australian National University (attested 1982) and as assistant professor at Kobe Shinwa University (attested 1996).

Hisashi Sato, a scholar of Tibetology and history/archaeology, studied at Kyoto University and became a professor there in 1968. He also served as a professor at Komazawa University and Toyo University, and held a post at Bukkyo University.

Hisataka Ishida works in Buddhist studies, Indology, and philosophy. He studied at the University of Tokyo and earned a doctorate from the University of Vienna under Helmut Krasser in 2011; he was a lecturer at Aichi Gakuin University (attested 2015).

Hisatake Kato was a philosopher who studied at the University of Tokyo (circa 1957–1961). He held positions at Yamagata, Tokyo, Tohoku, Tottori University of Environmental Studies, and the University of Human Arts and Sciences.
Hitoshi Inui is a Buddhist studies scholar who studied under Kanjin Horiuchi. He held posts at Koyasan University as a lecturer (attested 1986–1992) and later as a professor (attested 2015).
